Frances Foy (1890–1963) A key figure in Chicago’s progressive art scene, Frances Foy built a distinguished career as a commercially successful illustrator, painter, and printmaker. She later continued her training at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, where influential instructors George Bellows and Randall Davey helped shape her modernist direction. Foy began exhibiting in 1922 with the No-Jury Society of Artists and soon gained recognition from the Art Institute of Chicago. She and her husband, painter Gustaf Dalstrom (married 1923), were active members of Chicago’s Fifty-Seventh Street art colony and served as directors of the No-Jury Society. She also was featured in Art of Today: Chicago, 1933 , highlighting leading modernists of the era. During the 1930s, Foy contributed to federally commissioned New Deal mural projects and served on the Treasury Department’s Public Works of Art Project committee. Her mature work is celebrated for vibrant floral still life in oil and watercolor, alongside etchings produced at Hull-House. Foy’s legacy includes collaborative projects, notable exhibitions, and inclusion in prominent archives. Her papers are preserved at the Archives of American Art, Smithsonian Institution, underscoring her lasting impact on American modernism. 880019405704.title: Nippon Moriage Base Hand Painted Vases - Set of 2
880019405704.desc: - Description: Nippon Moriage vases. - Origin: Nagoya, Japan - Time Period: 1891-1921 - Condition: There are chips in the top of each vase - History: Nippon porcelain refers to items marked with "Nippon," which was required by U.S. law on imports from Japan between 1891 and 1921. During this period, Japanese porcelain manufacturers, particularly those in the region of Nagoya, produced a wide variety of decorative and functional items for export, with the United States being a primary market. These pieces are characterized by their hand-painted designs, often featuring floral motifs, landscapes, and intricate gilding. The term "Moriage" refers to the raised slip decoration, adding a tactile and visual dimension to the pieces. This particular vase showcases the aesthetic sensibilities of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, reflecting a blend of Japanese artistry and Western tastes. The handles and overall form are influenced by European styles, while the decoration remains distinctly Japanese, making Nippon ware a fascinating example of cultural exchange in the decorative arts.
